questions.stem: Why is DNA replication described as semi-conservative?

options.text: Each product DNA molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand
options.why: The two original strands separate and each becomes part of a product molecule alongside a new complementary strand.

options.text: Each product DNA molecule contains half of the original base sequence and half of a new sequence
options.why: Each product contains the full base sequence. The old and new halves are whole strands, not halves of the genetic information.

options.text: One product DNA molecule contains both parental strands while the other contains two newly synthesized strands
options.why: That describes conservative replication. In semi-conservative replication, both products receive one parental strand.

options.text: Both product DNA molecules contain alternating sections of parental DNA and newly synthesized DNA
options.why: That describes a dispersive model. Replication conserves each parental strand as one continuous template strand.

questions.stem: What does helicase do during DNA replication?

options.text: It separates the parental strands by unwinding DNA and breaking hydrogen bonds
options.why: Helicase opens the double helix so each parental strand can act as a template.

options.text: It adds complementary DNA nucleotides to the 3′ end of each new strand
options.why: That's the role of DNA polymerase. Helicase opens the parental DNA instead of building a new strand.

options.text: It joins adjacent Okazaki fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds between them
options.why: That's the role of DNA ligase. Helicase acts earlier by separating the template strands.

options.text: It removes RNA primers and replaces them with complementary DNA nucleotides
options.why: That's the role of DNA polymerase I in the prokaryotic system. Helicase doesn't replace primers.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the stages of one PCR cycle in the correct order?

options.text: Denaturation, primer annealing, extension
options.why: Heat separates the strands, cooling lets primers bind, and Taq DNA polymerase then extends those primers.

options.text: Primer annealing, extension, denaturation
options.why: Primers can't anneal to their target sites until denaturation has separated the two DNA strands.

options.text: Extension, denaturation, primer annealing
options.why: Extension needs primers already attached to separated templates, so it can't occur first.

options.text: Denaturation, extension, primer annealing
options.why: Taq DNA polymerase needs an annealed primer before extension can begin. Annealing must come before extension.

questions.stem: What determines the boundaries of the DNA region amplified by PCR?

options.text: The complementary sequences of the two primers
options.why: The primers bind on opposite strands at sites bordering the target region, so extension copies the DNA between them.

options.text: The positions at which Taq DNA polymerase denatures
options.why: Taq DNA polymerase doesn't define the target or denature DNA. Heating separates the strands.

options.text: The distance traveled by fragments through the gel
options.why: That distance reveals fragment length during gel electrophoresis. It doesn't choose what PCR amplifies.

options.text: The number of hydrogen bonds in the target DNA
options.why: Hydrogen bonds affect strand separation, but they don't set the endpoints of the amplified region.

questions.stem: Why is Taq DNA polymerase used in PCR?

options.text: It remains functional after the repeated high temperatures used to separate DNA strands
options.why: Taq DNA polymerase is heat-stable, so it can extend primers through many PCR cycles without being replaced after every heating stage.

options.text: It breaks the hydrogen bonds between DNA strands at a low temperature
options.why: High temperature separates PCR strands. Taq DNA polymerase adds nucleotides during extension.

options.text: It produces the RNA primers needed before every extension stage
options.why: Synthetic DNA primers are added to the PCR mixture. Taq DNA polymerase extends them but doesn't produce them.

options.text: It moves amplified DNA fragments toward the positive electrode
options.why: An electric field moves DNA during gel electrophoresis. Taq DNA polymerase works during PCR.

questions.stem: Why do smaller DNA fragments move farther than larger fragments during gel electrophoresis?

options.text: They pass more easily through spaces in the gel matrix
options.why: The gel acts as a molecular sieve. Smaller fragments face less resistance and travel farther in the same time.

options.text: They carry a positive charge that attracts them toward the negative electrode
options.why: DNA is negatively charged and moves toward the positive electrode. Fragment size affects movement through the gel.

options.text: They contain more base pairs and therefore receive a stronger electrical force
options.why: Smaller fragments contain fewer base pairs. Their advantage comes from passing through the gel more easily.

options.text: They are copied more rapidly by Taq DNA polymerase while moving through the gel
options.why: DNA isn't copied during gel electrophoresis. Taq DNA polymerase acts earlier if PCR is used.

questions.stem: Why does comparing more independent markers strengthen a DNA profile match?

options.text: It reduces the probability that an unrelated person matches every marker by chance
options.why: A chance match at one marker is possible. Requiring matches at many independent markers makes that explanation less probable.

options.text: It causes every DNA fragment from one person to become the same length
options.why: A DNA profile contains fragments of different lengths. More markers provide more points of comparison.

options.text: It proves that laboratory contamination couldn't have occurred during the analysis
options.why: Extra markers improve discrimination, but they can't rule out contamination or every other source of error.

options.text: It converts a pattern of DNA bands into the person's complete genome sequence
options.why: A DNA profile tests selected variable regions. It isn't a complete genome sequence.

questions.stem: In which direction does a new DNA strand grow?

options.text: From 5′ to 3′, by addition to its 3′ end
options.why: DNA polymerases add each incoming nucleotide to the free 3′ end, so the new strand grows 5′ to 3′.

options.text: From 3′ to 5′, by addition to its 5′ end
options.why: DNA polymerases don't extend the 5′ end. They synthesize new DNA only by adding to the 3′ end.

options.text: From 5′ to 3′ on the leading strand but 3′ to 5′ on the lagging strand
options.why: Both strands grow 5′ to 3′. The lagging strand is made in fragments instead of reversing direction.

options.text: In either direction, depending on the orientation of its template strand
options.why: Template orientation changes whether synthesis is continuous or discontinuous. It doesn't change the direction of polymerization.

questions.stem: Which feature is unique to lagging-strand synthesis?

options.text: Production as multiple Okazaki fragments initiated by repeated RNA primers
options.why: The lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously, so primase must provide a new primer for each Okazaki fragment.

options.text: Addition of complementary DNA nucleotides by DNA polymerase III
options.why: DNA polymerase III adds complementary nucleotides on both the leading and lagging strands.

options.text: Synthesis of new DNA in the 5′ to 3′ direction
options.why: Both new strands are synthesized 5′ to 3′. Direction alone doesn't identify the lagging strand.

options.text: Use of a parental DNA strand as a template for complementary base pairing
options.why: Both new strands use parental templates and complementary base pairing.

questions.stem: Which enzyme removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA in prokaryotic replication?

options.text: DNA polymerase I
options.why: DNA polymerase I removes each RNA primer and fills the resulting region with DNA nucleotides.

options.text: DNA polymerase III
options.why: DNA polymerase III performs most strand extension and proofreading. It doesn't replace the RNA primers in this model.

options.text: DNA ligase
options.why: DNA ligase seals nicks after primer replacement. It doesn't remove RNA or fill the region with DNA.

options.text: DNA primase
options.why: DNA primase makes the RNA primers. It doesn't remove them after strand synthesis.

questions.stem: What happens when DNA polymerase III detects a mismatched nucleotide at the 3′ end of a growing strand?

options.text: It removes the mismatched nucleotide and replaces it with a correctly matched nucleotide
options.why: This proofreading action corrects the terminal mismatch before synthesis continues, lowering the replication error rate.

options.text: It leaves the mismatch for DNA ligase to remove after replication finishes
options.why: DNA ligase seals nicks in the backbone. It doesn't identify or remove mismatched terminal nucleotides.

options.text: It separates both new strands and begins the entire replication process again
options.why: Proofreading corrects the individual terminal nucleotide. The completed parts of the strands aren't discarded.

options.text: It adds another nucleotide until complementary base pairing is restored automatically
options.why: Adding another nucleotide wouldn't correct the existing mismatch. The mismatched nucleotide must first be removed.

questions.stem: A DNA template has the sequence 3′-ACGTTA-5′. Which sequence is synthesized from it?

options.text: 5′-TGCAAT-3′
options.why: Complementary bases are added antiparallel to the template, giving T opposite A, G opposite C, C opposite G and A opposite T.

options.text: 3′-TGCAAT-5′
options.why: The bases are complementary, but the direction is written backwards. The new strand beside this template runs 5′ to 3′.

options.text: 5′-ACGTTA-3′
options.why: That repeats the template's base order instead of using complementary base pairing.

options.text: 5′-UGCAAU-3′
options.why: That is an RNA sequence because it contains uracil. DNA replication uses thymine-containing DNA nucleotides.
